 It sounds like the neighbor is simply being a bit cheeky and trying to intimidate you into doing something which would benefit him. You should be careful not to fall for such tricks, especially if he has been using the power supply since 2008.

question: A former CEO says that deleting a spreadsheet increases the value of the remaining spreadsheets. Is that how finance works?
answer:
I used to have an office full of old hard drives and paper files for old company information, all which were useless now. I was told not to delete any of them as they could potentially be useful in some way.
 Then one day I got into an argument with my boss over something I had done and he told me that if we didn’t do something about it then he would fire me.
 I was very upset at this point because I had been doing everything I was supposed to do so what did he mean by firing me?
 He said that if I did not fix the issue then he would fire me but I still didn’t understand how it related to anything I had done.
 He said he had a file on me and that the contents of that file were “confidential” and he couldn’t share them with anyone, including me. The next day someone told me that he had removed the contents from his file so I could have access to them.
 This made sense to me as well, he had no right to keep the information away from me when he knew he was going to fire me.
 Then one day he came back into my office and asked me what I thought of something I had done. I said I was glad I hadn’t done it because it would have cost me too much money to do it correctly and I was not going to waste my time on it. He seemed to be happy about this.
 A week later I found out he had been trying to get rid of some old hard drives and paper files that he didn’t need any longer and I was told that I should start looking for new ones so that I could replace them.
 I wasn’t surprised at all, he had always been trying to find ways to make things more efficient and less expensive.
 He then told me that he had decided to fire me because I had not followed the rules he had given me when we started working together. I said I thought he was wrong but he didn’t care and fired me anyway.
 I was very upset because I thought I had done everything I was supposed to do and now I had no job. Then one day he called me back into his office and asked me what I thought of something else I had done.
 I said it had nothing to do with anything I had done so why would he care about it? He said that it had been something I should have known about and that if I hadn’t known about it then I wouldn’t have been able to fix it correctly.
 This made sense to me as well, he had always been trying

question: My coworker forgot to say hello this morning. Should I be concerned?
answer:
I don’t think so, especially if it’s just a few people that she forgot to say hi to and not the entire office.
 However if she was in your office for the last couple of days and then suddenly didn’t show up until today, maybe you should check with her about what happened. Maybe she had an emergency or she wasn’t feeling well. It could also mean that she didn’t like working there at all. If that were true, she probably would have left long ago.
 In my opinion, she may have been tired and just forgot to say “Hi.” And the fact that she forgot to say hello doesn’t mean anything at all.
 But I do think she might have forgotten something else too. Like how to use a computer or what kind of work schedule they have here.

question: My wife and I disagree about what color to paint the kitchen. How should we decide?
answer:
The first thing I would suggest is to make a list of your favorite colors and share it with her. Then, make a second list of your least favorite colors and share that with her too. You can also show some pictures of kitchens with different colors on Pinterest to help you both get a feel for what each color might look like.
 You could also take a trip to a local paint store and sample a few of the colors in person before making a final decision.

question: My partner ate the last yogurt without asking. What should I do?
answer:
Do you have a “yogurt” or just plain yogurt?
 I have had yogurt for years and it has been an amazing addition to my diet. It helps keep me regular, healthy and full of energy.
 The reason that yogurt is so good is because it is a complete food that contains protein, calcium, vitamins A & D, potassium and fiber. These nutrients work together to keep your body functioning properly and make you feel great throughout the day.
 Yogurt is also very easy to eat because it doesn’t require any special preparation other than mixing in fruit or honey if desired.
 So why do we get upset when someone takes our yogurt without asking? Because we don’t want to share something that makes us happy with others who may not enjoy it as much.
 If your partner does enjoy eating yogurt then let them have some too! It will probably be better for both of you in the long run!
 And if they don’t like it then tell them so and stop giving them any more until they change their minds.

question: My manager used a period instead of an exclamation mark in an email. Is this a warning sign?
answer:
No, it is not.
 But I will tell you that in my experience people do use punctuation marks differently depending on their culture and language. For example:
 In English: "I am very excited about the project!"
 In French: Je suis très enthousiaste au sujet du projet!
 In Spanish: Estoy muy entusiasmado por el proyecto!
 So when I read an email from someone who speaks another language, I tend to pay attention to the punctuation they are using. If it is different than what I expect based on my own experience with English, I try to understand why they are doing this (is there a cultural reason?).

question: My friend returned a borrowed book with a different bookmark. Should I address this?
answer:
I'm sorry, but there is no good way to put it.
 If you want to be polite, just say "I noticed that the bookmark was changed" and then move on. But if you're going to give someone a hard time about it, then why don't you take their side?
 There's not much more you can do than that.

question: My coworker brought a different flavor of coffee than usual. Is this a sign they are unhappy at work?
answer:
I'm not going to say "Yes." I would assume it's more likely that your coworker is trying to spice things up, perhaps with an attempt at a new flavor profile for you and others.
 There’s nothing inherently wrong with having a different flavor of coffee every week (or even month). In fact, it’s the same thing as rotating a new recipe in the kitchen; if we’re being honest, most people will be more interested in how good the new flavor tastes rather than what flavor we’re actually drinking.

question: My partner and I disagree about which drawer should contain the spatulas.
answer:
I don't have any spatulas in my kitchen but we do have one in our bathroom. I think that's a place it belongs, so I'm going to move it there too! But you know what? I think it was an easy decision for me to make. I'm not even going to ask you how you decide when it comes to these things.
 It's been a while since I thought about this question. I've had many different kitchen drawers over the years, and they all had a different way of organizing the utensils. In fact, some of them were very messy. One drawer even had a lot of things stuck together by tape!
 That said, I still believe the best organization method is to use something that works well with the other things in your kitchen. For instance, if you have a lot of small things like spoons or forks, you might want to keep those in one place. If you have a lot of larger items like knives or saucepans, then maybe you should separate them out into their own drawers.
 The bottom line is that it's up to you what you think looks better. Maybe you prefer having everything in one drawer so you can easily find whatever you need when cooking. Or perhaps you think that having different things in different places makes more sense.
 No matter what, I hope you two get along well!

question: How do I prepare for a job interview?
answer:
Interview preparation is one of the most important stages in securing your dream job. The interview is your opportunity to show the employer that you have all the skills, knowledge and experience they are looking for. So, how can you prepare yourself properly?
Firstly, get an idea about what kind of questions will be asked during the interview. These may vary depending on the company and position you are applying for but generally include behavioural questions such as “Tell me about yourself”, “What motivates you?” or “Describe a time when you had to handle conflict.” In addition, there may also be situational or technical questions that relate directly to your field of expertise.
Once you have identified potential areas where questions might arise, it’s essential to develop well-thought-out answers using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). This ensures not only that you present your experience clearly and concisely, but it also allows employers to understand how you’ve handled various challenges in previous roles. For example, if asked to describe a situation where you faced a deadline crunch, make sure to detail exactly what happened, what your role was in this task, what actions you took in response and ultimately what results were achieved as a consequence of these efforts.
Secondly, practice mock interviews with friends or family members who can give feedback on both verbal delivery and body language aspects such as posture or tone of voice. Practicing will help build confidence when facing actual interviewers and ensure that you feel more prepared than ever before walking into the office space for your first day at work!
Finally don’t forget about researching thoroughly the company behind whom you are interviewing! Find out their mission statement, products/services offered and recent news stories related directly to them so you’ll be better informed ahead of time while answering questions asked during an event such as “Why do you want to join our team?”
In conclusion, thorough preparation leads to a higher chance of success in any job interview regardless if it is conducted virtually or physically through traditional means. By preparing answers using structured frameworks like STAR along with rehearsing mock interviews regularly and studying information gathered from previous events held by prospective employers there's no limit how far one could advance professionally given enough determination & effort!

question: What is the difference between market research and competitive intelligence?
answer:
Market Research: it's about finding out what customers are interested in. It's about understanding their needs, desires, motivations and behavior.
Competitive Intelligence: it's about finding out what competitors are doing, and how they are doing it.
The key difference is this: Market Research is about you; Competitive Intelligence is about them.
I don't believe a company can be successful without knowing who its customer is. But I also believe that companies need to know who their competition is and how they're winning at what they do, so they can figure out what makes their product or service different and better.
For example, if you were trying to sell me an iPhone X, the market research would tell you that I'm a fan of Apple products. The competitive intelligence would tell you that Samsung has released the Galaxy S10 which has a 6.3 inch screen, 8GB RAM and 512GB storage with a fingerprint scanner on the back.
If you only knew my tastes from Market Research, you might decide to offer me a larger phone with more RAM, but you wouldn't know about the Galaxy S10 until Competitive Intelligence told you it exists. So in this case, Competitive Intelligence tells you what you need to know so that your product can be better than someone else's product.

question: What is the difference between voltage and current?
answer:
Voltage is the potential energy per charge. Current is the rate of flow of charge.
 In a simple electrical circuit, electrons travel from negative to positive terminal through wires, creating an electric current.
 Voltage is measured in volts (V). The higher the voltage, the more potential energy each electron has.
 For example, a 9-volt battery gives the electrons enough potential energy so they can travel through a wire to power a small device such as a flashlight bulb. A larger voltage like 120 volts will have more potential energy than a lower voltage of 6 volts. But both will still produce current when connected to a closed circuit.
 Current is measured in amperes or amps (A).
 It is the rate at which charge passes a point over time, usually measured in coulombs per second.
 For instance, if you pass 3 coulombs of charge past a point every second, then you have a current of three amperes. If the same amount of charge passes in half a second instead of one second, your current would be six amperes.
 In general:
 Higher voltages produce higher currents through wires and resistors (for example, a 120-volt household outlet can deliver more current than a 6-volt car battery). But high voltage alone doesn't guarantee high current - you also need a complete circuit for current to flow.

I also know that if I don't show up, someone will miss me.

I could write this post on an app that is running in the background, or I could actually show up in person.

And it turns out that there's something really interesting about the first option.

It's called a feature freeze.

When a software team reaches a milestone, they lock down code changes to avoid breaking things.

The code is frozen. No new features can be added until after QA has finished and a release is approved.

So what happens during a feature freeze?

The developers are working to fix bugs.

They're doing unit testing, integration testing, security scans, performance analysis, user acceptance testing, etc.

This isn't glamorous stuff. It's not flashy like adding a new AI assistant.

But this work is absolutely essential for building high-quality software.

In fact, it might just be more important than new features.

And it also gives the team a chance to step back from the constant grind of writing code and reflect on their progress.

I'm reminded of that during a feature freeze when I see someone trying to make things better with a new chatbot feature.

But then I remember what it really takes: patience, discipline, attention to detail, and time spent fixing things that aren't quite right yet.

And sometimes, that's all you need to build something truly great.

question: My landlord says the mold in my apartment is load-bearing. Is this reasonable?
answer:
My landlord says the mold in my apartment is load-bearing. Is this reasonable?

Not at all.

Mold isn't a structural element or load-bearing wall - it's biological material that grows when there's moisture and organic matter (like wood, paper, etc.) present. In fact, if mold is truly growing on load-bearing structures like walls or ceilings, then we have a more serious issue: water damage leading to compromised structural integrity.

The real danger of mold growth is not structural collapse but health impacts for those exposed to mold spores. These include respiratory issues such as coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath, headaches, fatigue, nausea, and allergic reactions.

So yes, I did call an inspector. He confirmed the presence of mold in my apartment.

Now, he's also recommended I get an air quality test done. I'm going to follow through with this, because I'm concerned about how much mold is actually present and whether I am breathing it in every day.

But I can tell you that my landlord isn't a great fan of mold. So I'll be keeping an eye on him - he says he's working on the problem and will be sending me updates soon.

Nope! 

Electricity doesn't actually move downhill at all.

The speed of electrical energy is the speed of light through a medium (which for copper wire is around 20% of the speed of light).

It's the electrons themselves, however, that are moving at very slow speeds - typically less than a millimeter per second!

So even though there might be an electron flowing uphill in one wire while another flows down in another wire, the electrons don't travel fast enough to have much effect on the voltage or current going down the wire.

And when you connect two wires together, it's like connecting two different water pipes - they're both flowing water at similar pressure.

question: My neighbor claims he has tenure on my electricity supply because he has used it since 2008.
answer:
My neighbor claims he has tenure on my electricity supply because he has used it since 2008.

Not so fast.

The Electricity Act, 1998 provides that no person shall be deprived of his or her supply of electricity without a fair hearing and the opportunity to make representations (Section 34).

So what does this mean?

That I am not legally entitled to have electricity supplied through me, and I can only lose it if I don't pay my bills.

It is true that in most cases I will not receive electricity from a company unless I have paid all outstanding balances due with respect to the service. In other words, I have a financial interest in having power connected. However, there are some exceptions where I may be disconnected even if I have paid all my outstanding balance.

One example: when I am deemed to have used power illegally or unlawfully for purposes such as running an illegal business or operating unlicensed premises (Section 106).

The law makes clear that I have no automatic right to continue receiving electricity supply and I can be cut off at any time by a utility company if they determine that I am violating their terms of supply agreement.

I also need to ensure that I comply with the terms of my electricity supply agreement. If I breach these terms, I may face disconnection regardless of how much I have paid in fees.

So what can you do?

- Ensure that your electricity bill is up to date.
- Check the terms of your supply agreement to see if there are any restrictions on use.
- Contact the provider immediately if you suspect that you may be in violation of their rules or regulations.

By staying compliant with all applicable laws and regulations, you can avoid being disconnected from power and protect your rights as a consumer.

question: What is the difference between market research and competitive intelligence?

Market research and competitive intelligence are often used interchangeably, but they serve distinct purposes within a company's strategic decision-making process.

- Market Research focuses on understanding customer needs, preferences, behaviors, and overall market dynamics to inform product development, marketing strategies, and go-to-market initiatives.
- Competitive Intelligence, in contrast, delves into analyzing competitors' strategies, strengths, weaknesses, market positioning, pricing structures, product offerings, and innovation efforts.

While both approaches contribute to business success, it’s essential for executives to recognize that they address different aspects of the marketplace—market research centers around customers while competitive intelligence centers on rivals.
